Does this mean that al-Naẓẓām rejects the idea that sensory knowledge is a valid way of knowing the external world?
We have no direct statement from him that clearly answers this question.
Dr Albert Nasri Nader attributes to al-Naẓẓām the view that the error lies in the imagination rather than in sensation itself, because sensation cannot be wrong.
Dr Nader does not give a source for this claim. He may have inferred it from al-Naẓẓām’s statement that “the observer imagines…”—in particular, from the word “imagines.”
We doubt that al-Naẓẓām intended this meaning.

But even if we accept that the word can bear the meaning Dr Nader gives it, the first part of al-Naẓẓām’s statement says that “the senses judge otherwise.” Here al-Naẓẓām himself attributes the mistaken judgment to the senses, not to the imagination.

As for Dr Nader’s interpretation of this passage—that al-Naẓẓām means “the error of the senses here is an error in the whole, that is, in all judgments about particular things”—this reading likewise has no basis in al-Naẓẓām himself.

In any case, everything we have seen about sensory knowledge among the Muʿtazilites leads us back to the conclusion we reached earlier: in general, the Muʿtazilites accepted sensory knowledge as a valid way of knowing the external world.
By now it should be clear that the Muʿtazilites gave reason the highest place in the foundations of their system, and in the principles from which Muʿtazilite thought as a whole developed.

Their belief in human freedom of will is, at its core, one creative application of their basic view of reason. The same is true of the issue known in Muʿtazilite writings as “the question of rational good and evil,” which we will examine later in this study.

In fact, almost every question raised by the changing life of Arab-Islamic society in the Muʿtazilite period—whether it concerned doctrine, religious law, or human life—was approached by the Muʿtazilites through reason. They relied on reason to judge these questions, both in theory and in practice.

By now, this should be familiar enough that we do not need to spend much more time establishing it. What we need instead is to define, as far as the surviving Muʿtazilite sources allow us, what they meant by reason and by rational knowledge.
The first questions we face are these:
What is reason in Muʿtazilite theory? What does it do? And what are the limits of its ability to know?

The sources give us only a small number of passages in which the Muʿtazilites directly define reason. Even so, we can build up a broader picture from the many ways they apply reason when dealing with different problems.

The few direct definitions that have survived are concise and remarkably precise. They are enough to tell us a great deal. We also find many practical examples among Muʿtazilite thinkers, especially when they discuss things that cannot be known directly through the senses. These examples make it quite clear what they mean by reason, particularly when they speak about its role in knowledge.

We have two main definitions of reason before us. One comes from Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, and the other from Abū ʿAlī Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Jubbāʾī, a Basran Muʿtazilite who died in 303 AH/915 CE.
Al-Ashʿarī preserves al-ʿAllāf’s definition in three statements that complete one another and together form a single picture.

According to this definition, reason is “the power to acquire knowledge.” It is also “the power by which a person distinguishes himself from all other things.” And, he says, “we distinguish one thing from another through reason. We call sensory knowledge ‘reason’ only in the sense that it is something understood by reason.”

As we can see, this definition covers several things at once: what reason is capable of doing, how it works, what its role in knowledge actually is, what kinds of things it can know, and what kind of knowledge it produces.
First, reason is described as “the power to acquire knowledge.”
In Muʿtazilite terms, this means that reason can draw a universal idea from particular cases. As we have already seen, this is what the Muʿtazilites mean by knowledge.

If knowledge means discovering what a number of particular things of the same kind have in common, and then turning that shared feature into a general abstract concept, then reason is the power that allows a human being to make this discovery and carry out this transformation.
So this first part of the definition begins to tell us what reason does.
The second part takes us further. It says that reason is “the power by which a person distinguishes himself from all other things.”

This means, first, that a person becomes aware of himself. He then discovers what separates him from other things, and therefore what kind of relationship exists between the human self and the rest of existence.
From there, he can also discover the relationships between things themselves. As the third part of the definition says, we distinguish one thing from another “through reason.”
This gives us the second aspect of the definition: the function of reason.
The third aspect concerns the things that rational knowledge deals with.

From the definition, we can see that rational knowledge deals with abstract universals, with the self, with the relationship between the self and other things, and with the relationships between things themselves.
It also deals with “sensory knowledge,” which, as the definition says, we call reason only in the sense that it has been understood by reason.
This adds another function: reason turns sensory perception into abstract rational understanding.
The fourth aspect concerns the nature of rational knowledge itself.

The phrase “acquire knowledge” tells us that, for the Muʿtazilites, human knowledge is acquired through a person’s own activity and choice. It is not recollection, as Plato claimed. Nor is it instinctive or something that simply appears by necessity.
So in the end, Abū al-Hudhayl’s definition is less a definition of the essence of reason than a description of these four aspects of it.
Now let us look at al-Jubbāʾī’s definition:

“Reason is knowledge. It is called reason because through it a person restrains himself from things that a madman does not restrain himself from. The word is taken from the hobble used on a camel, which is called an ʿiqāl because it restrains the camel.”
This differs from the earlier definition in two ways.
First, al-Jubbāʾī says that “reason is knowledge” itself. Al-ʿAllāf, by contrast, says that reason is “the power to acquire knowledge.”
The difference is clear and important.

If reason is the power by which knowledge is acquired, then knowledge is the result produced by that power. But if reason is knowledge itself, then reason is no longer the tool that leads us to rational knowledge. It becomes the knowledge produced by the process.
There is one possible exception. Al-Jubbāʾī might be using the word “knowledge” to mean the act of knowing—the process by which knowledge is acquired—rather than knowledge as the final result.
But this seems unlikely, because if that were what he meant, the definition would no longer really define anything.
The second difference is that al-Jubbāʾī points to a practical function of reason. Reason guides a person’s conduct.
Al-ʿAllāf’s definition does not mention this.
Alongside these two definitions, al-Ashʿarī gives us a third, which he attributes to the Muʿtazilites in general rather than to any particular thinker.
It is almost identical to the first part of Abū al-Hudhayl’s definition:
Reason is “the power within a human being that enables him to acquire knowledge.”
We can therefore say that Abū al-Hudhayl’s definition expressed the general Muʿtazilite view of reason and rational knowledge in much the way we have just described.
Does everything we have said mean that knowledge of God falls outside rational knowledge and outside the work of reason, since none of the three definitions openly mentions it?
The answer lies in the kind of reason these definitions are describing.
They are concerned with theoretical reason—reason as “the power to acquire knowledge” through reflection and argument.

But in Muʿtazilite theory, theoretical reason belongs to the final stage of rational knowledge. The Muʿtazilites first divide rational knowledge into two kinds, and then place these within different stages.
Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, for example, says:

“Knowledge is of two kinds. One is necessary knowledge: knowledge of God and knowledge of the evidence that leads to knowledge of Him. Everything beyond these, whether it comes from the senses or from reasoning by analogy, is knowledge acquired by choice.”
This second kind is what we mean by theoretical knowledge, and it is the kind discussed in the definitions above.

Knowledge of God, by contrast, is classed by the Muʿtazilites as necessary knowledge. It is not produced through deliberate choice and acquisition, but through what they regard as the immediate self-evidence of reason.
In other words, it does not arise by turning sensory perceptions into rational concepts, nor through a process of abstraction based on logical argument and purely theoretical reflection.
The “evidence that leads to knowledge” of God rests on necessary or self-evident rational evidence, rather than on theoretical reasoning.
The Muʿtazilites also place knowledge of basic moral principles—such as good and evil and the virtues—among these forms of necessary knowledge.
From this we can see that, whatever kind of knowledge is involved—necessary or acquired, self-evident or theoretical—the final authority is reason alone.
They say, for example, that knowing God is required by reason.
Even the judgment that a person is obliged to know God therefore comes from reason itself. In this matter, reason is the authority they follow, not consensus and not scriptural verses.
Al-Shahrastānī confirms this conclusion when he says that the Muʿtazilites
“agreed that the foundations of knowledge and gratitude toward the Benefactor [God] are obligatory before revelation is heard.”
In other words, they are obligatory even before divine commands and prohibitions are revealed.
The difference between necessary knowledge and theoretical knowledge is therefore only a difference in the level at which reason operates, or in the kind of rational understanding involved.
This follows from the way the Muʿtazilites arrange the stages of rational knowledge.
Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf describes these stages through the example of a child.
At the earliest stage, the child knows himself through the senses. He notices that he has a body and a self, and that he experiences sensations through his body.

At the second stage, the child is not yet required to possess, all at once, complete knowledge of every aspect of divine unity and justice. But once he knows God’s unity and justice, he must also know everything God has required him to do.

Abū al-Hudhayl goes so far as to say that if a person fails to acquire all this knowledge at the second stage, and then dies in the third stage, he dies as an unbeliever and an enemy of God, deserving eternal punishment in Hell.
Al-Baghdādī reports him as saying that in this second stage, once the child has reached maturity, he must also “know through transmitted reports what can be known only through hearing.”

Al-Ashʿarī, however, reports Abū al-Hudhayl as saying that “maturity does not occur until reason is complete,” and that complete reason includes both “necessary knowledge” and “the ability to acquire knowledge.”
This means that rational knowledge begins only after a person has passed through the stage of purely sensory knowledge, when the senses alone are developing.
Once that stage has been passed, the person enters maturity—that is, the stage in which reason has become complete.
At this point, the two kinds of rational knowledge begin: necessary knowledge and acquired, theoretical knowledge.
From Abū al-Hudhayl’s statements as a whole, we can conclude that theoretical rational knowledge belongs to the third and final stage in the development of reason.

At this stage, a person reaches a new understanding of divine unity and justice, as the Muʿtazilites understood them. This understanding is now based on argument, evidence, and demonstration rather than simply on the first self-evident judgments of reason.
3 — The Idea of the “Two Inner Promptings” in Rational Knowledge
The Muʿtazilite view of rational knowledge also rests on an idea that explains how rational choice takes place. They called this the idea of the “two inner promptings.”

“Before revelation is heard, a thinking person finds within himself two promptings. One urges him to know the Creator, to thank the Benefactor, and to follow the paths of goodness and virtue. The other urges him toward the opposite. He then chooses what leads to salvation and avoids what leads to destruction. These two newly arising promptings that call him in opposite directions are expressions of the speech and inner conversation of the self.”
This shows that even the kind of necessary rational knowledge which Abū al-Hudhayl described as something “grasped by reason through reflection alone” still involves a process of human choice.
The Muʿtazilites were determined to preserve this principle of choice, not only in human actions but in the acquisition of knowledge as well.
This may explain al-Aswārī’s statement that a human being has a power that is equally capable of either of two opposites.
The principle of choice itself requires a person to stand in relation to both possibilities before choosing one of them.

At first there is hesitation between two inner promptings: one calls the person toward one course, while the other calls him toward its opposite. The person then ends this hesitation by choosing one of them.
The Muʿtazilites call the human ability to do either a thing or its opposite, before the final choice is made, capacity (istiṭāʿa).
Al-Naẓẓām explains the idea of the two promptings on this basis when he says:
“There must be two promptings: one commanding a person to act, and the other telling him to hold back, so that choice can genuinely take place.”

Again and again, whenever the Muʿtazilites discuss one of their basic principles or a question that follows from it, they make a point of defending human choice through the different theoretical principles on which their system rests.
This shows how strongly Muʿtazilite thought is marked by internal unity and coherence.
In our view, this is one of the features of a way of thinking deeply shaped by philosophical reflection and philosophical system-building.
In the passage from al-Shahrastānī quoted above about the “two promptings,” there was a brief reference to what the Muʿtazilites called “the speech of the self and its inner conversation.”
